title: The Vendor Finance Trap: Why Being Paid Over Time Means You Haven't Fully Sold Your Business
linkedin:
You agreed a sale price for your business. Part of that number won't actually land in your account for another one to three years.

That's vendor finance, a seller note the buyer repays out of the business's own earnings after settlement. It's common in owner-operated sales, especially when the buyer is management, family, or someone without deep capital behind them.

Here's the part most owners don't weigh properly before they sign.

Once settlement happens, every decision that determines whether that note gets repaid now belongs to someone else. Pricing, staffing, how tightly debtors get managed, whether the new owner takes on fresh debt. None of it sits with you anymore.

A soft quarter, or a new owner running working capital looser than you did, can show up as a late or renegotiated repayment. From outside the business, there is very little practical leverage to do anything about it.

Vendor finance is also usually subordinated. If things go wrong, the bank gets paid before you do, even though part of what is owed to you was meant to be your sale price.

None of this means vendor finance is a weak structure. It genuinely bridges valuation gaps and keeps deals alive that would otherwise stall. The difference is whether you treat the buyer as a borrower during negotiation, with security registered on the PPSR, consent rights over key decisions, and a term short enough that your exposure doesn't stretch across several trading cycles.

The sale price is the number everyone talks about. The structure behind it decides how much of it you actually keep.

You sell the business, agree a great price, and then find out part of it isn't paid until next year, or the year after.

That's vendor finance. The seller lends the buyer part of the purchase price, repaid over time out of the business's own earnings once it's no longer yours to run.

Sounds fine in theory. Except once settlement happens, every decision that affects whether that money ever gets repaid, pricing, staffing, how debt gets managed, now belongs to someone else.

If you've sold a business this way, or you're weighing up an offer that includes it, how carefully did you look at the security behind it before signing?

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria who are weighing up an offer to sell, or who have already agreed one with part of the price deferred.

That deferred portion is usually structured as vendor finance, where the seller lends part of the purchase price back to the buyer and gets repaid over one to three years out of the business's own future earnings. It's common in owner-operated sales, particularly when the buyer is existing management, a family member, or someone without deep capital backing.

The detail worth understanding before signing is that once settlement happens, every decision affecting whether that repayment actually lands, pricing, staffing, how the new owner manages debt and working capital, no longer sits with the seller. Vendor finance is also usually subordinated, meaning the bank and other secured lenders get repaid first if things go wrong.

None of this makes vendor finance a poor structure. It genuinely helps close deals that would otherwise stall. The difference comes down to whether the terms treat the buyer as a borrower, with proper security and a sensible term, rather than simply a counterparty.
